entry: Global financial crisis centered on U.S. mortgage-backed securities, 2007–09. Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) tied to U.S. [[Real estate|real estate]] and related [[Derivative (finance)|derivatives]] collapsed in value from 2007, and the liquidity crisis spread to global institutions by mid-2007. The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 triggered a stock market crash and bank runs in several countries. The crisis deepened the [[Great Recession]] and contributed to crises in Iceland and the eurozone. It followed lending to low-income borrowers with high-risk subprime loans, which regulators largely did not police. Governments responded with bailouts, including the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program. Some 8.7 million U.S. jobs were lost. The Dodd–Frank Act of 2010 overhauled U.S. financial regulation, and it was weakened in 2018.

Domestic terrorist attacks in [[Norway]] on July 22, 2011. Far-right extremist [[Anders Behring Breivik]] detonated a car bomb in [[Oslo]]'s government quarter, killing eight people, then about two hours later shot 69 people at a Workers' Youth League summer camp on the island of Utøya. The 77 deaths made it the deadliest attack in Norway since [[World War II]]. In 2012 Breivik was convicted of both attacks and sentenced to 21 years of preventive detention, the maximum penalty in Norway, with possible indefinite five-year extensions.

Undersea [[Megathrust earthquake|megathrust earthquake]] and [[Tsunami|tsunami]] off Japan's northeast coast, March 11, 2011. At moment magnitude 9.0–9.1 it was the most powerful earthquake recorded in Japan and the fourth most powerful in the world since 1900. Waves may have reached 40.5 m (133 ft) at Miyako, Iwate Prefecture. Official figures from 2021 reported 19,759 deaths and 2,553 missing. The tsunami caused meltdowns at three reactors of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant. Economic damage was estimated at over $300 billion, the costliest natural disaster in history.

Explosion of 2,750 tonnes of [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate]] at the port of [[Beirut]], Lebanon, on August 4, 2020. The chemical had been confiscated in 2014 from the [[Cargo ship|cargo ship]] MV Rhosus and stored at the port for six years without adequate safety measures. A fire in a nearby warehouse ignited it. The blast killed at least 218 people, injured about 7,000, and displaced some 300,000. Estimated property damage reached US$15 billion, and Prime Minister Hassan Diab resigned on August 10.

Military seizure of power in [[Myanmar]] on February 1, 2021. The [[Coup d'état|coup]] by the Tatmadaw deposed the elected National League for Democracy government, detaining State Counsellor [[Aung San Suu Kyi]] and President Win Myint the day before the new Parliament was to convene. The military declared the November 2020 election results invalid and transferred power to Min Aung Hlaing. Armed resistance led to a civil war, and reported deaths reached at least 50,000 by March 2024. Independent analysts regarded the charges against Aung San Suu Kyi as an attempt to legitimize the seizure of power.

American film production and distribution studio owned by [[The Walt Disney Company]]. Founded in 1935 as Twentieth Century-Fox through the merger of Fox Film Corporation and Twentieth Century Pictures, it was one of the major studios of Hollywood's Golden Age. [[Rupert Murdoch]]'s News Corporation acquired it in 1985. Disney bought most of 21st Century Fox's assets in 2019, and the studio took its current name in January 2020 to avoid confusion with Fox Corporation. Its library includes *The Sound of Music*, *Titanic* and *Avatar*.

Western art music composed from 1901 to 2000. The century had no dominant style. [[Claude Debussy]] led Impressionism in France, while Gustav Mahler and Richard Strauss extended post-Romantic symphonic writing. In Vienna, [[Arnold Schoenberg]] developed atonality and then the twelve-tone technique, which his followers Alban Berg and Anton Webern extended. After World War I, [[Igor Stravinsky]], [[Sergei Prokofiev]] and [[Maurice Ravel]] wrote neoclassical works that drew on earlier forms. Serialism, electronic music, *musique concrète* and aleatory techniques were all developed during the century. [[Minimalism]] emerged later, and [[Jazz|jazz]] and folk music became important influences on many composers.

Annual endurance sports car race held near Le Mans, France. First run in 1923, it is the oldest active endurance racing event in the world. Unlike fixed-distance races, the winner is the car that covers the greatest distance in 24 hours. The Automobile Club de l'Ouest organizes the race on the Circuit de la Sarthe, which combines closed public roads with racing track sections. It is part of the FIA World Endurance Championship. In 1988 a car reached 407 km/h (253 mph) on the main straight, which led to added chicanes.

American counterterrorism thriller television series, 2001–14. Created by Joel Surnow and Robert Cochran for Fox, it stars [[Kiefer Sutherland]] as federal agent Jack Bauer. Each season covers 24 consecutive hours in real time, shown with split screens and an on-screen clock. The series ran 204 episodes, including the 2014 limited series *24: Live Another Day*. Critics objected to its depictions of [[Torture|torture]] and its portrayal of Muslims.

Timekeeping convention dividing the day into 24 hours from midnight to midnight. Times run from 00:00 to 23:59. It is the most commonly used time notation in the world and the format of the international standard ISO 8601. Many English-speaking countries, including the [[United States]], generally use the [[12-hour clock]]. In [[Medicine|medicine]], the 24-hour clock is generally used because it avoids ambiguity about when events occurred. The notation 24:00 marks the exact end of a day.

Bright quasar in the constellation Virgo, identified in 1963 as the first quasar. It is the visually brightest quasar in the sky, with an apparent magnitude of 12.9, and lies about 2.4 billion [[Light-year|light-years]] away. Its central [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] has a mass of roughly 900 million solar masses. The quasar is a prototype of an [[Active galactic nucleus]], powered by material falling onto that black hole. It lies at the center of a giant elliptical galaxy. Its jet, about 200,000 light-years long, was imaged by the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and emits synchrotron radiation from relativistic particles. Its luminosity varies at nearly every wavelength.

Construction of three-dimensional objects from digital models by adding material, usually layer by layer. Material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control. In the 1980s the techniques were used mainly for prototypes, and by 2019 some processes had become viable for industrial production. Complex shapes, including hollow parts and internal lattices that reduce weight, can be made that would be impractical by hand. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which extrudes a thermoplastic filament, was the most common process as of 2020.

Second-largest object in the [[Asteroid belt|asteroid belt]], after [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]]. Discovered by Heinrich Wilhelm Matthias Olbers on March 29, 1807, it has a mean diameter of 523 km (325 mi) and makes up about 9% of the belt's mass. It is the brightest asteroid visible from Earth. [[NASA]]'s Dawn spacecraft orbited it from July 2011 to September 2012. Meteorites from its surface, the howardite–eucrite–diogenite (HED) group, have fallen to Earth.

Anonymous English-language imageboard website founded in October 2003. Created by Christopher "moot" Poole as a counterpart to the Japanese Futaba Channel, it hosts boards on topics from [[Anime|anime]] to video games and politics. Users typically post without registration, and threads are ephemeral. The site had more than 22 million unique monthly visitors as of 2022. It helped popularize [[Internet meme|memes]] such as lolcats and [[Rickrolling]], and it has been influential in hacktivist movements such as Anonymous. Its lax moderation has made it a focus of controversy over harassment and illegal content.

American rapper, actor, and businessman. Born in [[Queens]], New York City, he was struck by nine bullets in 2000, which led Columbia Records to cancel his debut album and drop him. [[Eminem]] signed him to Shady Records after discovering his 2002 mixtape. His debut album, *Get Rich or Die Tryin'* (2003), debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and produced the hit single "In da Club". He has sold more than 30 million albums and later produced the television series *Power* (2014–2020).

Sex position involving mutual oral sex between two partners at the same time. The name refers to the partners' bodies, which resemble the numeral 69. It is a translation of the French *soixante-neuf*, a term first traced to the 1790s in France. The [[Kama Sutra]] mentions the position under another name. The position can be awkward for partners of different heights.

American convenience store chain headquartered in Irving, [[Texas]]. It began in 1927 as the Southland Ice Company, selling ice from storefronts in [[Dallas]]. The 7-Eleven name, reflecting hours of 7 a.m. to 11 p.m., was adopted in 1946, and franchising began in 1961. Ito-Yokado, a Japanese supermarket chain, acquired a controlling stake in 1991 and full ownership in 2005. The chain operated about 85,000 stores in 20 countries and territories as of August 2024.

Four coordinated Islamist suicide bombings on [[London]]'s public transport during the morning rush hour of July 7, 2005. Three bombs exploded within 50 seconds on [[London Underground]] trains, and a fourth destroyed a double-decker bus in Tavistock Square. The attacks killed 52 people from 18 countries and injured nearly 800. They were the deadliest terrorist incident in Britain since the 1988 bombing of [[Pan Am Flight 103]]. The bombs were made from concentrated [[Hydrogen peroxide|hydrogen peroxide]].

1963 Italian avant-garde comedy-drama film directed by [[Federico Fellini]]. Its Italian title is *Otto e mezzo*. [[Marcello Mastroianni]] plays film director Guido Anselmi, who suffers from creative block while preparing an epic science fiction film. The metafictional narrative moves through dreams, memories and fantasies involving the women in Guido's life, portrayed by Claudia Cardinale, Anouk Aimée and Sandra Milo. Shot in black and white by Gianni Di Venanzo, with a score by Nino Rota, it won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film and Best Costume Design (black-and-white). The British Film Institute ranked it 10th in its 2012 Sight & Sound critics' poll.

American independent film and [[Television|television]] production and distribution company, founded in 2012. Based in New York City, it was established by Daniel Katz, David Fenkel and John Hodges. It is known for arthouse films and for influencing contemporary [[Horror film|horror]]. *Moonlight* won the Academy Award for Best Picture, and *Everything Everywhere All at Once* (2022) won Best Picture and six more Oscars. Its television programs include *Euphoria* and *Beef*.

Swedish [[Pop music|pop]] group formed in [[Stockholm]] in 1972. Its members were Agnetha Fältskog, Björn Ulvaeus, Benny Andersson and Anni-Frid Lyngstad. A win at the [[Eurovision Song Contest]] in 1974 with "Waterloo" brought international fame. Hit albums and singles followed, and as the members' marriages ended, their later music became more introspective. The group disbanded in December 1982. Their songs formed the basis of the stage musical *Mamma Mia!* (1999) and its 2008 film. ABBA's sales exceed 150 million. The group reunited for the album *Voyage* (2021) and the virtual-avatar residency ABBA Voyage in London (2022).

Group of three Dutch-administered islands in the [[Caribbean Sea]], north of [[Venezuela]]. Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire are the westernmost islands of the Leeward Antilles. Aruba and Curaçao are autonomous constituent countries of the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands]], and Bonaire is a special municipality of the Netherlands. The Dutch West India Company established a major port on Curaçao and imported enslaved West Africans to the island and to Bonaire. Abolition in 1863 devastated the plantation economies of Curaçao and Bonaire. Oil refineries, built after oil was discovered in Venezuela, supported the Allied war effort in [[World War II]]. Aruba separated from the Netherlands Antilles in 1986, and the Antilles were dissolved in 2010.

Australian rock band formed in [[Sydney]] in 1973. Founded by brothers Angus and Malcolm Young, the band has been described as hard rock, blues rock and heavy metal, and calls its music simply rock and roll. Its 1980 album *Back in Black* was recorded after lead singer Bon Scott died, and it is one of the best-selling albums of all time. The band has sold an estimated 200 million records and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2003.

Italian professional football club based in Milan, founded in 1899. The club plays in [[Serie A]] at the San Siro stadium, which it has shared with [[Inter Milan]] since 1947. Milan has won 19 league titles and seven [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup/Champions League]] titles, second only to Real Madrid. Under Silvio Berlusconi's 31-year presidency, the club won 29 trophies, and in 1991–92 it won the Serie A title without a single defeat.

Connectors linking devices to [[Alternating current|AC]] mains electricity. The plug is attached to the device and inserts into a socket connected to the circuit. Plugs and wall sockets for portable appliances appeared in the 1880s, and three-pin earthed plugs about 1910. Standards differ by region: the [[United States]] uses plugs with two flat blades, while much of Europe uses round pins with side earthing clips. Adaptors connect incompatible sockets, though they may not provide full safety.
